newsitem.title: USA: Rap record label faces probes, other troubles.
newsitem.headline: Rap record label faces probes, other troubles.

text.p: Death Row Records has consistently topped the rap music charts during its four-year existence, pulling in $300 million in sales and making the black-owned record label an emblem of the American dream.

But since one of Death Row's biggest stars, Tupac Shakur, was shot and killed in September, Death Row has faced one problem after another -- including the jailing of owner Marion "Suge" Knight, a federal investigation, litigation over Shakur's estate and the departure of its accountants.
For Knight, who worked his way up from a black working-class community to become a wealthy record executive, the recent attention is not what he craved when he formed the rap label four years ago.
"There are all kinds of facts coming to light and this is the beginning of the end for Death Row," said one record industry official who requested anonymity.
Knight, whose label's youthful stars such as Shakur and Snoop Doggy Dog have had repeated brushes with violent crime, has been on probation himself since 1995 for a 1992 assault.
Last month his probation was revoked for allegedly taking part in the beating of a gang member in Las Vegas just hours before Shakur was gunned down on Sept. 7.
Knight has been in prison in Chino, Calif., since Dec. 13, a spokesman for the state Department of Corrections said.
Adding to Knight's legal woes are questions regarding Death Row's financial dealings.
According to people familiar with the case, Steve Cantrock of Coopers & Lybrand, Death Row's former auditors, has gone into hiding after threats to his life.
The auditing firm, which no longer works for Death Row, said in a statement it was cooperating with the investigation into the record label's dealings.
"Coopers & Lybrand is aware that Death Row Records and its Chief Executive Officer Marion Knight are being investigated by various law enforcement agencies," the firm said.
A spokesman confirmed Cantrock was on leave and all of Death Row's financial records handled by Cantrock have been turned over to investigators.
Federal prosecutors are investigating Death Row for alleged racketeering and links to street gangs, violent crime, drug trafficking and money laundering, sources familiar with the case said.
Federal officials in Los Angeles and Las Vegas, where the probes are being conducted, declined to comment. But sources said the probes may result in criminal indictments in coming months.
Death Row and Knight's attorney, David Kenner, were unavailable to comment.
Despite strong sales, Death Row has never turned a profit due to repayment of debt and Knight's extravagent spending habits, lawyers and other sources said.

"We believe Death Row withheld royalty payments from Tupac and failed to deliver advances promised under his contract," said attorney Richard Fischbein, who represented Shakur's mother, Afeni, in a court battle this month that forced the label to stop selling unauthorized Shakur merchandise.
"Tupac was one of the most successful artists, but had nothing to show for it the day he died," said Fischbein.
He said that, despite albums sales of $60 million this year, Shakur allegedly owed Death Row $4.9 million at the time of his death.
"From here on in, we're seriously investigating what else is due the estate. It's just the beginning," said Fischbein.

Further controversy swirled around the label in September when it was revealed that the 18-year-old daughter of Los Angeles Deputy District Attorney Lawrence Longo, who had overseen Knight's probation, signed a $50,000 record contract with the label this year.
"Longo's on paid leave and a personnel investigation is ongoing relating to his relationship with Kenner and Knight," a spokeswoman for the Los Angeles District Attorney said.
A parole hearing is set for February for Knight, who may face up to nine years in prison, according the L.A. District Attorney's office.
